utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. There are three matters I'd like to deal with before we begin today. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there is a matter to be raised, we will bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Robinson, there is a discussion among the parties as to the scheduling of witnesses? Could you put it on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. After the direct examination of Mr. Krajisnik concludes, which we hope will be today or tomorrow morning, we would propose to insert three witnesses who have already arrived here in The Hague to be testifying. That's Mr. Puhalic, Mr. Poplasen and Mr. Kupresanin. Actually Puhalic, Kupresanin and then Poplasen is the order. And then we expect that that would take the balance of the week and then on next Monday, because of commitments by the counsel for the next witness, Mr. Brdjanin, we would propose to interject his testimony and then resume the cross-examination of Mr. Krajisnik either late Monday or Tuesday of next week, when Mr. Brdjanin completes his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been agreed upon with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And has the witness been informed of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you once again and remind myself that we have to make sure we make breaks. I wanted to ask you as I'm not sure whether we have established that or not, when did you become a member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a member of the Main Board in 1991. I think it was on the 12th of July of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember my speech given on the 15th of October, 1991, before the meeting ended, and the speech had to do with the adoption of a memorandum on the sovereignty by the other two communities, a memorandum which is often quoted and cited here as an example of threat and war mongering on my part.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber how did you experience this speech? What was your impression and understanding of it when you heard it live as the parliament speaker at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it as a warning, and an expression of concern with regard to a process that was then ongoing in which certain issues would be resolved in an unconstitutional manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, could we have the exhibit number of that speech, either in terms of page number of the transcript or whatever? If anybody could assist us. But let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, we have heard that speech on a number of occasions here. When I said that they should not follow the same highway as Slovenia and Croatia as they would lead Bosnia to hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, did this speech of mine wish for or encourage the Bosnian Muslim and Croatian side to go to hell and was it an instance of war mongering?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can elaborate on this expansively, if need be, but now my answer will be brief. I really understood that this was a speech of warning, actually, and a great wish to reach a solution, but with a warning that unfortunately what did eventually happen could happen, that a war could break out and that unwanted subsequences could occur because the road of secession in an unconstitutional manner, according to these words as I understood them, and as it was explained to me later with regard to this speech, that manner in which the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be resolved was not the right one. Nor could it lead to a final solution that would satisfy all the parties. And eventually the aim was also to prevent the war which could be seen everywhere around us at that point as a possibility, a possible outcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: D267 is the exhibit number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that -- I'm trying to stick to the time line, Mr. President, so as to make things easier for you. I think that we are now past January 1992, the proclamation of Republika Srpska, the preparations for holding the referendum? Could you tell us what do you know about barricades which were set up in Sarajevo on the 1st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last time I noted that here, as far as I remember, all three delegations were at negotiations somewhere abroad. I believe it was in Brussels or perhaps Geneva, because these two places were the locations where we held most of the talks. And on our return, I believe that our delegation was in Belgrade when we heard the news about the barricades. And what caused the putting up of the barricades? It was the murder of a member of a Serbian wedding party, actually the bride groom's father was killed in the Sarajevo Old Town, in Bascarsija, which caused a spontaneous revolt on the part of the Serbian people, also great fear and concern, because through history, something like that used to happen in the darkest periods -- actually, could not happen even in the darkest periods of our history in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It happened immediately after the referendum which had been held, and then the barricades and counter-barricades that were later put up practically put all of Sarajevo in a blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn then or later in what way and at what point did the Serbian Democratic Party become involved in resolving the problem of the barricades? Was there a Crisis Staff before that and after that, at the central party level? Did it exist?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time that it was only then, for that occasion, that the Crisis Staff was formed. As far as I remember, Mr. Rajko Dukic was then the self-proclaimed, if I may put it so, president of the Crisis Staff. Ms. Biljana Plavsic was another personality from the Serbian leadership. And at this level, they were attempting in contact with the other side to resolve problems. Your Honours, you can find the minutes from the meetings attended by Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Ejup Ganic, Mr. Dukic, Ms. Plavsic, and there was an attempt to reach and find a solution, so I could say that the involvement of the Serbian Democratic Party was in this spontaneous revolt. At the head of the revolt was the Crisis Staff, which was appointed for that specific occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Bosnia survive this unrest from early March and could you tell us, even though you already spoke about this, what sort of events filled the month of March, in terms of the meetings between the parties and the European Community and also the activities of the Serbian representative bodies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricades and the problems that followed after the murder of the member of the wedding party and the blockade of Sarajevo, this was all something that I was involved in as well, practically all of Bosnia-Herzegovina political establishment was actively engaged in this. And, of course, the key issue was resolved at the level of the three parties which made the partnership: The Party of Democratic Action, the Croatian Democratic Union and the Serbian Democratic Party. The tensions eased off when this crisis was overcome. In fact, what followed was a continuation of negotiations and bilateral and trilateral meetings of the parties, and then we held the first meeting that had to do with negotiations under the auspices of Mr. Cutileiro, and then the second meeting as well. As far as I remember, it was on the 11th of March; and then the second one on the 17th of March. Please don't hold it against me if these are not the exact dates. I'm certain about the 17th of March. So March was a period of negotiations and a month in which we managed to come up with a high quality solution which was supposed to bring an end to all the tensions, and we continued the activities aimed at reaching an agreement that would resolve the destiny or, rather, the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, as for the implementation of this solution, and the realisation of this agreed plan, was war necessary for that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was the greatest chance for Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think that there was not a single reason to have war, and we can see that best if we compare that solution from the 17th of March with the final Dayton agreement. There are minor differences between the two. If I want to be precise, I think that the side which declined the Cutileiro Plan, I mean the Muslim side, perhaps got less by the Dayton agreement than it would have gotten if Cutileiro's principles had been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've come to the moment when I have to ask you something about the indictment against me and also the one against you, about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise that we wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we've made objections to this kind of question before, because it involves the -- it's an attempt to elicit from the witness legal opinion. It's the underlying facts which are significant, and that's what Dr. Karadzic should be turning his attention to. So before he elaborates this kind of position, I want to again object to efforts to elicit from witnesses legal analysis and legal opinions which do not assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't yet heard the question. Let us see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is whether a joint criminal enterprise existed on the Serb side, with the objective of creating an ethnically pure Serb unit or Serb state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had an objection pending that was a mere effort to circumvent the objection. That's why I made it in advance so it would be clearly on the table. So now the issue is joined. The exact scenario that I anticipated was coming from the introduction of that question was realised and therefore the objection stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether a joint criminal enterprise existed on the Serb side, with the objective of creating an ethnically pure Serb unit or Serb state. So that's a legal formulation, in your opinion, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think simply the words "joint criminal enterprise" could be changed to an "agreement" and it would satisfy Mr. Tieger, but I think everybody understands and by now joint criminal enterprise and a layman's point of view. But if Mr. Tieger objects, then Dr. Karadzic can simply ask if there was an agreement to do this and we can accomplish the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be a fairer question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, now you spoke about the Cutileiro Plan and you said that war was not necessary. Did we have an agreement to create an ethnically pure Serb territory, Serb entity, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to create an ethnically pure territory without war and if the Lisbon agreement had been applied?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side accepted Cutileiro's principles at the talks on the 17th of March. And it is with full responsibility that we wanted to implement these principles. Had we implemented these principles, everybody would have reached a compromise in terms of the requests coming from all sides. There was no reason for anyone of the sides involved to opt for war instead of these principles. Because if we wanted to have a delineation, not borders, among the three national or ethnic units, without war, it is totally senseless for someone not to accept principles based on peace and then say, No, we don't want to do it that way, we want to go to war, and then to have a lot of people killed, which is what actually happened. I'm saying this from the position of the Serb side, and I believe that not a single one of the parties involved should have opted for that, if they accepted Cutileiro's principles truly, in good faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Speaker, before the war, and without war, did we create any plans about population resettlement or population expulsions of members of any other religious or ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any such plans. However, may I just add one single sentence or perhaps two? In terms of the review proceedings that I'm working on right now, I collected a great deal of information about my role and the role of the Serb side. These activities show unequivocally that the only task was to find solutions, especially you, as the leader of the Serb Democratic Party. That can be seen from the documents, from the evidence there. At the very beginning of the war - how do I put this? - you made a very conciliatory speech at a session held on the 27th of March and you called upon Members of Parliament to find solutions in order to preserve peace. And you said that peace was actually a major interest of our people. So I tried to find a document, as I investigated my own case, to see whether there was a document that was falsified, forged or perhaps misinterpreted by someone. I didn't even find a wrongful document like that. Up until the very last evening I was in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had we had any kind of plan, I would have left the assembly two or three or I don't know how many days before that, and I would have started working on the implementation of this plan that is being imputed now. You can see this from the abundance of evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a brief question in relation to staying on in Sarajevo. Can you remember until when Professor Plavsic stayed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Mrs. Plavsic remained in Sarajevo about 15 days after the war broke out, if I remember correctly. I stayed on too, truth to tell, in the Serb area, so to speak. However, she remained in Sarajevo where the Muslim side was dominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out -- I beg your pardon. The proposed plans and discussions before the war, did they envisage the existence of other communities in the Serb unit, in the Muslim unit, in the Croat unit, and how were their rights supposed to be exercised? I'm referring to the Cutileiro Plan and also to our negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen easily from the documents. There were several persons who took part in the discussion, especially President Karadzic said on several occasions, invoking tradition, especially Montenegrin tradition, when there is supposed to be an attitude of valour, that is to say to treat with dignity those who are less capable. So all of those who needed to be protected. The Cutileiro Plan and our policy was that there should be reciprocity. If Serbs remain in Muslim-Croat areas they should be protected, and also Muslims and Croats in our area. So everything I'm saying does exist in evidence and it can be found easily in documents. So it's not only that Mr. Karadzic spoke about this. How do I put this? This was a unanimous view expressed by all of those who were in parliament. Those who were belligerent, these were simply emotional outbursts, words that were not well measured. However, if people were to remain as a minority in another area of the sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they should have all their religious, ethnic and other rights protected. This can easily be found in documents in statements before this Tribunal, evidence before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out, did we ever envisage that there would be no Muslims and Croats in the Serb Republic of BiH or in Republika Srpska after that? And did we ever envisage that we would not allow refugees to return once there were refugees?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen in statements, by way of evidence, that we always envisaged that there would be certain areas in the Serb unit that would be populated by other ethnic groups, as a majority, particularly in some of the enclaves in the western part of Republika Srpska and elsewhere. Because in some of these areas, the absolute majority -- or, sorry, relative majority was members of the other ethnic group, the other people. Also, there were certain areas in the middle, if I can put it that way, the Muslim ethnic area. And they were supposed to be an enclave, let me call it that conditionally speaking, Serb enclave. Ozren is a good example of that, that was surrounded by many Muslim municipalities, and it was an area where there were 100.000 Serbs. So what we envisaged for Muslims and Croats is what we expected for the Serbs in the Muslim and Croat ethnic areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the indictment it is alleged -- actually let's do it the other way around so we do not upset Mr. Tieger. When did the Serb Democratic Party come to power and how long did it remain in power?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party came to power in the elections of 1990, held in November 1990. As far as I can remember, that's when the elections were held. And it had a relationship of partnership with the two other national parties until the 5th or 6th of April, 1992. That was a period of a bit more than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the indictment, it is alleged that we -- oh, I beg your pardon. Until when? Until when was the Serb Democratic Party in power in Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you just be a bit more precise? Are you referring to the period before the war or during the war, even after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until when, on the whole, was the SDS in power in Serb areas, in Serb communities? How was there a replacement or, rather, when were new elections held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. All the way up until 1996, the first post-Dayton agreements, there was a war going on and the Serb Democratic Party was there. The first post-Dayton elections held from 1996 to 1998, the Serb democratic power was in -- the Serb Democratic government -- party was in power, in government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02173, could we please have that on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the indictment, there is this allegation that I was in charge of a joint criminal enterprise that started with a violent take-over of power in the municipalities that are listed there, ultimately it is less than 20 municipalities. Who was in power and for how long, say, on the 31st of March in Bijeljina and who was in power on the 31st of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijeljina, as one of the municipalities, from the beginning of the elections, November 1990, all the way up until the end of 1998, it had a government of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that's not the number. 1D20173. 20173. Thank you. Could we have the English version as well, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, this is the 4th of July, 1995, Bosnia-Herzegovina, sent this message to Vasvija Vidovic, who was a delegate before this Court. In this document, there is a description of the way in which the Serb side took power, and please look at the third paragraph that has to do with Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the text that is being read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka, just like Bijeljina, from November 1991 onwards, it was the SDS that was in power in the Municipal Assembly, or, rather, a coalition headed by the SDS; whereas in Bijeljina, it was the Serb Democratic Party that had absolute power. So it is illogical that now, when the war started, somebody should take over because power was in the hands of the SDS even before the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the second page displayed now, or rather, the end that refers to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says in the indictment that we totally cleansed the Serb areas of Muslims and Croats. And now look at the last line here. It says in the territory of the municipality of Banja Luka, there are still about 10.500 persons of non-Serb ethnicity left, 7.500 Bosniak Muslims and 3.000 Croats. This is Mr. Nedzad Ugljen. The late Mr. Ugljen who was killed later on. He certainly reduced the number. But even according to his dour assessment, would it be true that we had cleansed Banja Luka of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not correct, and I can just add something by way of a small comment. I know from my own proceedings, that there was this report of some people from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I did last week, I'm going to ask that the accused refrain from commentary during the course of his questions. He certainly reduced the number, according to his dour assessment, this is the accused not only leading but testifying and it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, it may reduce the probative value elicited from the witness. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we have the following page in the English version of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before Bosanska Dubica, you can see some figures that we have already discussed. Mr. Speaker, could you please tell us or finish what you have just started about the presence of Muslims and Croats not only in their own enclaves but also in the cities all the way up to the end of the war? And this is the beginning of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that somebody should have been a magician in order to establish how many of the representatives of what population remained in what -- in certain areas. However, some people took it upon themselves to send reports that they imagined to be good, and then Mr. Tieger knows what kind of reports those were, and there was one such report that was totally unrealistic. However, he believed -- that person believed that he had to brag about something and say that that was an area where there were indeed Muslims and Croats and that it was a pure area, as he put it. This is an erroneous piece of information that misled many to conclude that a major campaign of ethnic cleansing had been carried out in those areas at the very start of the war. I know for a fact, and documents corroborate that, that a large number of Muslims and Croats, and especially Muslims, remained in Banja Luka even after the end of the war. There were also, in Banja Luka, Muslims at the beginning of the war, throughout the war. So to say the least, this kind of statement was biased, and it was issued in order to meet the requests of some people who wanted to portray the situation as ethnic cleansing on the part of the Serbs or paramilitary units. You will see exactly how many Serbs there are in federation, how many Muslims in the cities and areas in Republika Srpska. I'm sure that we will be able to prove that at the end of this case. I have information that that picture is totally, totally different than is portrayed here before this Tribunal based on such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now look at page 4 in Serbian? We are talking about the municipality of Laktasi. What page is it in English, let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, while you are saying that other reports may be biased, how could you say that this figure is correct which we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I apologise. I don't know about the credibility of any such reports. I am speaking from my own experience and I'm saying that what was happening during the war were magnified eventually. So what I'm saying is that one has to take this report by Mr. Ugljen very cautiously. I know that there were a lot of Muslims and that a small number of them stayed in Banja Luka as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that a small number stayed in Banja Luka or, rather, let me put it in a different way: Do you know any town in Republika Srpska which was completely cleansed of Muslims, where Muslims had lived before but were expelled during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing comes to mind. Maybe they all left. I don't know. I can't remember. Nothing comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Speaker, do you know of entire settlements in Republika Srpska which are purely Muslim or predominantly Muslim which remained so until the end of the war, and where the Muslim population remained living safely?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there are such settlements. Documents corroborate that. Members of the Muslim and Croatian peoples were even members of the VRS. As far as I can remember, such things happened in Gradiska and in the western parts of Republika Srpska. Those people lived peacefully and they were members of the army that defended Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at page 4. We are looking at page 3. Mr. Speaker, do you know of a place or a settlement in the Muslim-Croatian federation where the Serbian population survived September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that a certain number of Serbs did remain living in the federation, as ethnic hostages, let me put it that way. There was torture, the conditions of life were very bad and the Serbs wanted to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, according to the prevalent policies at the time, the departure of the Serbs was big business, and the Croats were those who enabled the Serbs to leave in the direction of the Serbian part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what was the destiny of Bradina, the Serbian village in depth of their territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Tribunal, that village was part of an indictment, all the people from Bradina and the surrounding settlements were arrested and taken to prisons, and in this Tribunal, those prisons are called camps. The entire families were prisoners, irrespective of the fact whether any one of them had arms. As a matter of fact, they were all -- or, rather, the only criterion for their arrest was whether they were Serbs or perhaps members of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the ultimate lot of Bradina, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really remember. I don't know what happened, but I learned here, at the Tribunal, that all of the people were either killed or ended up in prisons where they were ill treated. There is a book by Strahinja Zivak who described all those things that happened around Konjic and Bradina where people were mercilessly killed or ill treated or they went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the logic of this document. Look at the municipality of Laktasi, for example, where it says that there were 82 per cent Serbs, 9 per cent Croats and 2 per cent Muslims, and that the others made up 8 per cent and the reference here is to Yugoslav. It says here the political control of the municipality, given its majority Serbian population, was already seized in early April 1992. When was the political control seized over the municipalities with a Serbian majority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already spoke about that. From the elections in 1992, Laktasi, which had an absolute Serb majority, had a Serbian government, and all the way up to 1998, conditionally speaking, although that period of time is moot for this discussion. So it is really not logical to say that the aggressor, which is a derogative word for the Serbs, i.e. that the Serbs took over Laktasi on the 4th of April. Laktasi had already had a government, it had an authority, so it really doesn't make sense if we were to follow the wording of the text that is before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the Serbian page, we can see Kotor Varos. I'm interested in just one sentence. Do you have an explanation as to why the conflict started only on the 11th of June, which means nine weeks after the war broke out in Sarajevo? It was only on the 11th of June that the conflicts started in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this is an example of a municipality where the local representatives of the three ethnic groups tried to find a solution, either by way of the -- politically dividing the municipality or in some other way, all with a view to avoiding a war. If the local representatives had been able to decide on that in those municipalities, there would never have been a war. As far as I can remember, those municipalities received a dispatch from Sarajevo, and the agreement that had been reached was violated and that's when the conflicts broke out. Croats and Muslims joined a large armed force and then crimes happened. I'm speaking from memory, but I'm almost sure that this was the course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I'm tendering this document which will be very instructive in terms of the logic of charging the Serbs. Even Nedzad Ugljen admits that Croats and Muslims existed in all of those municipalities in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D20173 receives Exhibit D4002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to word my next question really carefully because I'm talking about taking power and taking over power. Can you explain the Trial Chamber how do you interpret the term "taking power" and "taking over power." In pre-trial brief, paragraph 3, it says that the physical take-over of power took place in a number of municipalities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, when the three ethnically based parties won the elections, then the authorities or the sectors were split between three ethnic groups. However, each of the parties was supposed to take power from the previous government, from the communist government. Throughout 1991, it was a turbulent year, full of political skirmishes. The Serbian Democratic Party could not take power. The old cadre still kept power and they were representatives of the League of Communists. They fought very hard to keep that power and they wooed the ethnically based Party of Democratic Action promising them to be loyal all in order to remain in their positions. The Serbian Democratic Party was prevented from taking power. Your Honours, you can see that from various telephone conversations, where it was insisted on the members of the Serbian Democratic Party to be assigned their positions. However, it was only done at the very top. At the lower levels it was impossible to take power. And how do I understand the term taking over of power? And the taking over of power is as it is explained in the indictment. It is a violent take-over of something that doesn't belong to them. And that should involve war and armed rebellion or something. For example, you saw the examples of Banja Luka, Laktasi and Bijeljina. There was no need to take over power. The Serbian Democratic Party had power, it took power based on the results of the election, and any take-over of power would have been an unnecessary adventure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The indictment against me, counts 1 through 8, charges me with pursuing a policy which was aimed at creating a Serbian entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as establishing and leading those political organs that would pursue that policy by way of committing crimes. When it comes to the creation of a Serbian entity, was it envisaged that that entity would be created by war and by committing crimes? Who was it who suggested that we should have a Serbian entity? Who agreed with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I've already talked about that, but let me repeat. The first piece of information that reached me coincided with the information that the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina would have its ethnic entity in return for giving up on our idea of Yugoslavia, and that came from the representatives of the international community. The information reached Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic, and they, in turn, told me. A few days later, at a meeting in Belgrade, that was elaborated by Mr. Milosevic. Soon after that, Mr. Cutileiro explained his principles and said it clear and loud that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be split into three different ethnic entities, and among those there would be a Serbian entity. This means that from the international community, we learned that we would be given our own ethnic entity or national entity. What we learned was also learned by Mr. Milosevic, and he shared that information with us at that meeting in Belgrade. After that, reluctantly albeit, we gave up on the idea of Yugoslavia and we accepted the only realistic possibility, and that was to be given our own entity within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us where the first Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina was held, when it was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first founding session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina was held in the building of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a hall which was called the blue hall which was assigned when we distributed the space to the Serbian deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it done secretly? Was it a secret session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a secret session. There were many guests, and some of those who came to check out what that was all about were the representatives of the other ethnic groups, but they only stayed there briefly and then went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, were Serbian political bodies such as the council of ministers, after the proclamation of Republika Srpska, were these bodies established secretly or so that the public could not see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was done publicly, transparently. I had talks with representatives of the other two ethnic groups, held in the parliament. I explained to them what our intention was. We only advocated that we should set up the organs that we had the right to have according to the Cutileiro Plan, and that was endorsed by all three sides, and that the others would have as well, which was eventually implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina later on through the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember who made up the council of ministers and was it envisaged for the council of ministers to have the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence initially? I'm not talking about the government but the council of ministers.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cutileiro Plan envisaged that there should be joint organs and that there should be the organs of the entities. What we did then was that from the existing ministers or deputy or assistant ministers who were Serbian representatives, were the ones that we used to set up the council of ministers. I would not exclude the possibility that perhaps not all of them were there but I can guarantee that more than 95 per cent were the representatives from the joint organs, those who were appointed to the council of ministers. That was how we understood the Cutileiro principles and how we implemented them in practice. We said there would be joint organs. In the joint organs which we now really have because we had Bosnia-Herzegovina, we would take the deputies from them, like from the parliament, and our representatives from the council of ministers would articulate our requests and our views in the government, just as the deputies or the MPs would define the Serbian interests in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the goal, and that was eventually implemented once the council of ministers was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the existence of Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence was envisaged for the council of ministers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was envisaged. I forgot to answer to that part of your question. It was envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anyone appointed to these positions? I'm not talking about the government but the council of ministers, which was envisaged earlier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, in fact, in the council of ministers, the minister of MUP of Republika Srpska should have been appointed, and eventually it was indeed implemented once the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the joint government, the joint single government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you remember who of its members were members of the Serbian Democratic Party and its leadership and who were not its members?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if I can be 100 per cent precise but certainly more than 90 per cent. Except for one member of the government, the late Velibor Ostojic, minister of information, everyone else was a member. They may have been former communists or they may have had a neutral political position but the only representative of the government in the council of ministers was Mr. Velibor Ostojic. There may have been somebody else but I can't remember now, perhaps one or two people, but everybody else was a non-member of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information about their positions with regard to the functioning of the joint government and what was their position and the conclusion of the Serbian members of this government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like the MPs were outvoted in the parliament, the members of the government kept complaining that the positions which were allocated to the Serbian party, the people could not be assigned to them in practice, and that the government was trying to resolve economic problems and problems that were important for the life of ordinary citizens, it was impossible to do that. The government was polarised, there was a great rift within the government, even though I have to say that the then prime minister, Mr. Pelivan, was a man who was really attempting to achieve cohesion and to lead the government forward, but he was unsuccessful in that because there was a tendency to count people, to see who was in which party; therefore, the government was overly politicised and eventually solutions were imposed on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the situation is like with the joint government in Bosnia now?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, today, there are still significant rifts within the government. Each part of the council of ministers, as the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is now called, is a story for itself. Now they take into account who is a member of what party rather than of what ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, it's relevant insofar as this is a standard, that's the character of Bosnia as a state. Outside of the federation, that's how it lives its life. It was not something that was defined by the Serbian Democratic Party in 1990 or 1991. The Serbian Democratic Party is not in power at the central level now. It is others who are, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please stick to relevant questions. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 1D01402. If there is no translation, I will have to apologise and I apologise to the Prosecution that perhaps I may not have announced this document in advance. Thank you. Could you -- I believe that the translation is available somewhere but I'm not sure in which form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber -- have a look at what this document is and then tell us whether at the time you received this document too?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title of this document is: "Note from the meeting of officials and leading employees of the republican state organs, the cadres of the SDS BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just scroll down so we can see the date, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 12 of December --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 12th of September - interpreter's correction - 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we initiate or request this meeting or was it the initiative of the Serbian ministers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though there are many things that I don't really remember well any longer, I remember one particular meeting, and I believe that this is a note from that meeting. It was held at the initiative of the ministers who were members of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I know that there was heated discussion, there were many irregularities about the representation of Serbian interests and the interests of the Serbian Democratic Party in the government and all irregularities which existed with regard to appointments and what was happening within the government and what it was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have found the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please place it on the ELMO. We have the English translation. Thank you. Can we please see the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you remember whether Miodrag Simovic, who was the vice-premier of the federal government and who was on the list of the Serbian Democratic Party, was he a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page, please. Next page in the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we'll move more efficiently and certainly more accurately if the accused bears in mind that this is apparently the same document as 65 ter 11295 which has the English translation already uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we try that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for your kindness. It's really helpful. Can we please show that in e-court. [In English] Next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I will ask you to look at the document because I will ask you a question that summarises all this. Were you aware of the difficulties that the Serbian staff in the joint organs complained about, the difficulties with regard to implementing the agreement, appointing Serbian personnel and so on? Were we pressing them with regard to this or were they pressing us and complaining that they could not implement what they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. Individually, some of the ministers came to see me in the parliament, so I am aware of all the problems which are listed here, at least on this page, the appointment of cadres and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the following page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, can you just remove the transcript? Because it's off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last page, please, both in English and in Serbian. Perhaps that's not in this document, or it could be two pages earlier, please, two pages earlier, where the conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we can see it here. Let us stay here because we can see who it was sent to: Yourself, Plavsic, Koljevic, Cancar and Dukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, Koljevic, Cancar and Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back two pages, please. No, two pages forward. Two pages backwards, actually. The following page, where the conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on paragraph 3, in the record, to suggest to the leadership that the following conclusions were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you interpret the fact that in September 1991, nine or ten months after the establishment of the joint authorities, the Serbian cadres, who were mostly not members of the SDS, could not discharge their functions and requests from the SDS to implement the agreements with the other two sides?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is evidence that throughout the previous period, those ten months, the personnel from the circle of the Serbian Democratic Party or, rather, the Serbian people were not appointed to their positions, which they got after the distribution of positions on the basis of the agreement between the three ethnic communities. But this also tells something else, namely that this was the preparation for the following month, in which the declaration would be adopted by voting and practically any will of the Serbian people to participate in the authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina on an equal footing be disqualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit number D4003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One of the items contained in the indictment -- or, rather, paragraph 11 of the pre-trial brief, says that Karadzic, as far back as 1990, warned that efforts made by the Bosnian Serb -- Bosnian Muslims and Croats to change the nature of the Bosnian state would be responded to by force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there legitimate and legal ways of changing the nature of the Bosnian state? Could it have been changed without our consent?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina envisaged the way in which a recomposition could be carried out, if I can put it that way, or the way in which a different fate could be determined for Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the only way in which the question of the destiny of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the coming period could be resolved. In the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is what I said in my testimony before, there were -- Serb MPs accounted for more than one-third of the parliament. If I can put it this way, our partners on the other side, those who wanted to secede from Yugoslavia, who wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to secede from Yugoslavia, could not carry this through in parliament because they did not have enough MPs for a two-third majority. However, the only way in which this recomposition could be carried out, or rather how the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina could be resolved, would be through parliament or through a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me not enumerate all the persons who are referred to as members of the JCE: Milosevic, Karadzic, high officer -- high ranking officer of the JNA including Mladic, Jovica Stanisic, Seselj, Arkan, not to mention all of them. Can you tell us what you think about this group? Did it act in unison? Did they constitute an enterprise? What were our relations like and what were our political views within this group that is referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have a -- obviously a particular problem with the question, what was -- what were our relations. I take it that means your relation and my relation as a kind of joint team with any of the individuals involved named in this group. But the introduction which sort of spells out its relationship to some aspect of the pre-trial brief or the indictment is an another reflection of Dr. Karadzic's continuing inability to refrain from signalling the witness what he wants from the projected answers. But as far as just asking about relations, that's how the question could have been phrased in the first place, and that's how they should be formulated in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's a helpful suggestion. Are you going to reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, it is being held against me -- it is being stated that I was a member of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic can just ask the question without prefatory comments about what the impact of any answer might be or about what his concern about the information at issue or sought is. That was the nature of the earlier objection, which the Court endorsed, and again he can simply ask questions that seek information in an objective way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no difficulty if you just refer to the indictment, or passage in the statement, but formulated as you did, it may sound as if you are feeding the witness. I think you can simply ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the programme-based or political closeness was among these persons who are mentioned as members of the JCE, including president Milosevic, high officers of the JNA, Mladic, Seselj, Arkan and others who are referred to as key participants?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the programme-based differences or the political differences among the participants who were members of various political parties were enormous, especially the ideological differences that existed. They were quite big. I can say, for example, that members of the JNA were heirs of the communist ideology from the previous period. Mr. Milosevic belonged to that ideology, too, to a large extent. Mr. Seselj was -- how do I put this? The SDS, on first glance, was close to the Serb Radical Party, but it was a political opponent, for winning over this patriotic bloc, if you will. Other participants were people we did not even know. We had just heard of them distantly. I can state with full responsibility that the only common denominator for these persons is that they were all Serbs. It is very hard to find any other common denominator. Secondly, had this been a joint criminal enterprise with the objective of attaining some objective in a time that no one could have presumed would happen, that is to say that war would happen and that certain ethnic areas would be cleansed by force --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your knowledge, in order to attain ethnic division, did I intend to destroy the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats and were those selected for that living in the areas that the Bosnian Serbs had laid claim to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with certainty, and I have quite a bit of evidence, or to put it in better terms, I have practical examples, the President of Republika Srpska at the time, Mr. Karadzic, was absolutely far away from any kind of thinking along those lines. I'm just going to give one example and that is present before this Court. The Croat people had been expelled from the area where they had clashed with the Muslim army. It was primarily Mr. Karadzic's decision with the consent of the others who were in the top echelons of power. They passed through our territory without any incidents involved. They were saved from grave, very grave, consequences and they went to the territory that they wanted to go to. As for the Muslims, again, we have many individual examples, not the kind of example that we have in the case of the Croats, except for Western Bosnia where individual cases were being treated with maximum humaneness, in order to protect the unprotected Muslim people. I know that as I studied my own example. And with all due respect to the Office of the Prosecutor, I think that they made a big mistake there, putting this kind of diverse group together into some kind of joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the joint assembly, and in the assembly of the Serb people, there was an MP, Miladin Nedic, and he was quoted in the indictment and in paragraph 30 of the pre-trial brief as saying, and that is 65 ter 00028, page 40, so I'm going to quote what is being quoted there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the note -- the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "As for what is happening in Bosnia, I'm not in favour of having it resolved in haste, just like that. We have to admit that the Muslims were being planted in front of us so that we would be their executioners. I don't want the Serb people to be executioners, but also I'm not in favour of handing over our country, our state, our territory." And then a bit further on: "Therefore without any haste, because we are a people who has now been given this role of executioner in order to do someone a favour." Can you tell me how you understood this statement made by deputy Nedic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to correctly interpret this statement, perhaps some experts, linguists, should explain that, those who are familiar with the rhetoric that is resorted to there. And perhaps they should also know the MP in question. He was an epic type of person, Mr. Nedic. When he spoke, he spoke in a certain way but it was a serious statement this time. He usually spoke in a very witty way, but this time he said that somebody had persuaded Muslims to go to war instead of resolving the crises in Bosnia-Herzegovina by peaceful means. And in that way, the Muslims were planted there, if you will, so that somebody would kill them, abuse them. And he said someone gave the Serb side, the Serb army, a particular role to play. And now they are engaged in a battle with the Muslims and they are their executioners, he said. This is his opinion, that someone persuaded the Muslims to go to war, and in that way put them in a position to be killed. And then he says, We should not allow ourselves to be tricked in that way, that somebody gave us a role on behalf of somebody else's interests so that we could behave in an incorrect or inhumane way. That was his view. That is how he viewed the situation, why the Muslims went to war against the Serbs. Because several times he said that we were similar peoples in many ways, and there is no reason for us to kill each other, nationally or ideologically. He didn't want to be misunderstood because there was a war going on, so it would seem that he was defending the Muslims who were committing crimes against the Serbs because that's what the propaganda said, too. And he said that that does not mean that we should allow Republika Srpska to disappear. That is my view. I'm convinced that that is correct, but perhaps somebody could write a proper paper on this, explaining this kind of situation, knowing who Mr. Nedic is, knowing all the details and knowing how he articulated this. I must say it was not only he. This was a view shared by many MPs and also ordinary people who did not belong to parliamentary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My position was also quoted; namely, that I said this conflict is there so that the Muslims could disappear, that we fuelled it. What was your understanding of this? Who did we hold accountable for the fuelling of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe this answer is just going to be a continuation of the first answer I gave. What you said, what you stated, this was actually an articulation of a far broader opinion, if I can put it that way, that the Muslims, again if I can put it this way, were stimulated to go to war and that because of their interests, somebody was pushing them into war against the Serbs and without any proper grounds because all of this could have been resolved by peaceful means. Now, who is it specifically? Who is the one who was supposed to be the one who was instigating the Muslims to do that? I can give you my opinion now. And I think it is being shared by those MPs who then presented the same views or similar views. There were many external mentors in our situation and we know that that happened on the Muslim side too. The diaspora, the international community, international people in different ways, "great Muslims," under quotation marks, who were charting this course of the Muslims fighting to the last Muslim. I really would not want to speak about people who are deceased, but the then-ambassador of America in Belgrade, Mr. Zimmerman, very often I referred to that example, that he exercised this influence at the crucial moment, for them to refuse the Cutileiro Plan and this led to war. Now, I don't know how correct that is. That should be investigated. But there were such opinions, and that then, in fact, you articulated something that was part of the public opinion, and also of the many debates that were taking place. There was actually the external factor that stimulated this. Although later on, and we knew it at the time too, many people within the Muslim national core, if you will, in positions of high responsibility in their government, they rejected any kind of peace agreement, and in this way, they were seriously pressurising Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Izetbegovic. The best example is their assembly in Zenica. Sometime in 1993, when the Owen Stoltenberg Plan was rejected, there were several variants there then, and very little was required at that point in time to have the war brought to an end. After all, everything had already been spelled out in the Cutileiro Plan. So my opinion is that there were people from the outside who seriously exercised influence over the Muslim leadership so that they would continue the war rather than work for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The indictment suggests that the Army of Republika Srpska was responsible for using military means in order to achieve the six strategic goals. What was your position on that or what is it now? And let me quote one of the first interviews given by General Milovanovic. He was interviewed by the OTP. I accept, I accept. First the answer and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let us see the indictment passage first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is paragraph 48 of the pre-trial brief. I transformed this into a word document so the numbering of the paragraphs may have been altered as a result of that. I'll quote: "For the implementation of the strategic goals, it was the VRS and General Mladic who were primarily in charge of that. General Mladic said at the assembly what we are supposed to do. This should be a secret. Mladic and his officers transformed those strategic goals into the operative goals for the VRS and spent the following few months in implementing the plan and liberating the territories that belong to us by right."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, what can you say about this claim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a continuing objection, and in this guise, I want to not only reiterate it but reinforce it. It's inappropriate, in my judgement, for the accused to bring in his closest crony, present him with selected portions of the pre-trial brief or the indictment, and then seek his opinion or view or position on the manner in which or the evidence which has been marshalled regarding his case. Mr. Krajisnik was a contemporaneous participant in the events, as we know. There is no reason why the accused can't ask him for his information at the time, his observations at the time, about aspects of the case that he considers significant. I think this general objection has been sustained in other contexts and in various forms. I continue to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's take a sentence, for example, the first sentence of pre-trial brief, paragraph 48, primary responsibility for implementing the strategic goals fell to the VRS and General Mladic, who told the assembly in the closed meeting that the thing we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret. So asking the witness to make his observation on this sentence, what problem would there be, in your opinion, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, had it been done in that way rather than a lingering and continuing practice of identifying portions of materials in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief which Dr. Karadzic is concerned about, and obviously eliciting, trying to elicit from this witness some information to the contrary, then I might not object to the identification of various pieces of information as points of departure for eliciting information from this witness. But in the context in which the accused does it, I don't think it's appropriate. Yes, I don't think there is a tremendous amount of difference between saying, Do you recall what General Mladic said at a particular assembly with respect to X and identifying this particular -- a particular portion, but that's not what's happening. What's happening is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, what he did this time was after reading out paragraph 48, he asked, What can you say about this claim?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After contextualising it for this witness's benefit in the manner that he considers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As coupled with his comment that, for example, saying that to the effect the indictment suggests Army of Republika Srpska was responsible for using military means in order to blah, blah. But I -- I just intervened and then I told him to show the exact passage. After that he showed -- he read out paragraph 48 and asked what Mr. Krajisnik could say about this claim. On that basis, we can continue, can't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can continue at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So for your benefit, I read out the paragraph 48 again: "Primary responsibility for implementing the strategic goals fell to the VRS and General Mladic, who told the assembly in the closed meeting that the thing we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret. Mladic and his commanders turned the strategic goals into operational imperatives for the VRS, moving forward in the coming weeks and months to cement existing gains and move further toward 'liberating territories which by birthright are ours.'" So do you have any observation on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can explain the genesis of the six strategic goals. I testified about that in the Popovic case. I handed over all the documents to the OTP, those documents testifying to the way how the six strategic goals were generated. Those were not the military tasks of the army. That is my first observation. Second of all, you can look at the map which was presented to Cutillero and you can compare it with the six strategic goals, and you will see that most of the strategic goals in that map were actually proposed, and if we add to that the agreements reached with the sides in the meantime, we will see that the six strategic goals were our realistic plan -- I beg your pardon, not our plan but our desire as to how they could be achieved by political means. What did Mladic mean? What did he think when he said that that -- they should be kept a secret? He is here. He could explain. At those meetings, he never explained that. He never gave any broader elaboration of the fact. What is correct is that very often during the war, soldiers tried to give a different meaning to their statements. They exaggerated the role of the army in one way or another. That's why he used the word "secret." However, at our meetings, I never heard a secret that would be related to any of the things that are suggested here. And, particularly, you should look at something that happened before the army was set up. Look at the map. Every ethnic unit actually took up its ethnic borders with slight corrections. The army only corrected some things or lost some territories or gave a different physiognomy to that map. The form of Serbian ethnic existence at the beginning and at the end differs very little, so the army protected the areas. It didn't conquer those areas. So my interpretation or position or conclusion, if you will, is that this is an erroneous conclusion. The army did not have a task to implement those goals because those goals were political goals that were publicised, presented to the international community, and there was no reason whatsoever to give them a cloak of secrecy. There is evidence to that effect. There are documents. Many of the documents are part of the case law in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up D01598 in e-court. This is General Milovanovic's interview given on the 27 March 2001. I'm interested in page 5 in Serbian. I will also like the relevant page to be displayed in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to read: "General Milovanovic then said that the Tribunal should not try to prove the character of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina through such trials. At the beginning of the war, the Serbs wanted, above all, to stay in the SFRY. The Muslims wanted to form their Muslim state. And the Croats wanted to access to the Drina River. At the beginning of the war, he asked the leadership at the time to provide objectives of the war which were the following: To protect the Serbian people from destruction in order to avoid a repeat of events that took place between 1941 and 1945; and number two, to stay within Yugoslavia, or, as an alternative to this, have our own state." Mr. Speaker, are you aware of any other tasks that we may have given to the army? What do you think about what General Milovanovic said in this interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic's statement is completely correct. I don't know of any other objectives or goals, nor do I think that there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the establishment of the Supreme Command, you were far from any military developments. Still, can you tell us whether the leadership requested from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I hope it's clear what the problem is. I mean, now he's purporting to testify for this witness. Before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I wanted to make things easier for the speaker. I wanted to make it clear for him that I know that he doesn't have direct knowledge of any military events. However, do you know that the leadership tasked the army with conquering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are further complicating the process, delaying, wasting, making us waste time. You are not giving evidence on his behalf, "I wanted to make it clear for him that I know that he doesn't have direct knowledge ..." Inappropriate, an inappropriate comment on your part. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Okay. Let somebody say that. Would a legitimate question be this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we, as a leadership, ask the army to occupy those territories where Muslims and Croats made up a majority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such examples. However, in order to be more precise, I would like to say that certain areas or certain territories where Muslims made up a relative majority, for example, Gorazde, where there were a lot of Serb detainees, and where there was fighting going on for those areas, but that was not at the request of the political leadership. It was a move that was forced in order to protect the Serbs or allow them to retreat from those areas. So there were no requests made on behalf of the leadership to take Sarajevo. The Serbs had a large armed force, there were a lot of Serbs in Sarajevo, there were a lot of requests by individuals to occupy Sarajevo in order to liberate the Serbs there. The leadership headed by Mr. Karadzic who was the then-president of the republic made it clear that we wouldn't be interested in taking all of Sarajevo. We just wanted to have part of Sarajevo with our settlements and with Serb majority, that was the policy we pursued all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, do you remember the 13th of May and what happened in Banja Luka a day after the assembly meeting and the march of the Special Police forces? Did you attend that meeting? Do you remember any of the speeches made at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of meeting [as interpreted], it was a day after the first assembly meeting of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., in Banja Luka. There was a line-up of the policemen there, and the chief of that centre stated in his speech, and he was one of the speakers there, he said that a lot of their members were Muslims and Croats, and that they were proud of that fact. There was a round of applause and we were all glad to hear that because the Serbs had a majority there but that was what reflected the policy of the Serbian Democratic People and the Serbian people. We wanted to behave correctly wherever we were a majority, and we wanted to protect national minorities in all such places. In that sense, and there are documents to corroborate that, I saw them a long time ago, Mr. President, Mr. Karadzic's speech was along the same lines as well as all the other participants. I believe that the mayor of Banja Luka also spoke at that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I speak as well, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.
