You delivered a speech along those same lines, and the message was clear to the Muslim people, that they should feel safe and comfortable, that there was no reason for them to fear anything, and that they should not succumb to the influence of the fundamentalist circles among their people, that she should not commit crimes, that they should lay arms, that they should be loyal to the city and the -- where they lived and the authorities that the city was under.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: D005 -- 494 is the following document. I don't want to call it up. I'm just going to read a part of my speech on page 4 of the transcript of the video-clip where it says: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, to our greatest sorrow, and against our will, one part of the leadership of the two other people imposed a war on us. We are exterminating ourselves and we are torturing ourselves. And this was also imposed on us. We are trying to take the least part in that as possible. At times, for an hour or so, we do not return fire. We only return fire when we feel really jeopardised. Further on, it says: We have decided to proclaim unilateral truces for the whole world to see who is it who breaches those truces. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, we are not in conflict with Croats or Muslims. We are in conflict with the militant leaderships who want to impose their own state on us, where they will dominate and where they will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, I would like you to upload the document for the benefit of the interpreters. It's very difficult to interpret when you read out something without seeing the document. I would like to know the exact reference. What's the exhibit number of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D00494, page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to my e-court, it says it's a transcript of testimony somebody in Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think -- I'm looking at it in e-court. It says video Banja Luka parade D494, exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, I looked up the P exhibit. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be uploaded, please, page 4. [In English] In English I suppose it's also page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Speaker, it's in the bottom, towards the bottom in Serbian, and perhaps the next page in English: We in Bosnia are not in a conflict with Muslims and Croats. We have a conflict with militant leaderships who wants to impose their state where they will be dominant and where we would be second-rate citizens. That is to say an escort people to the leading people which was communicated to us in clear fashion on some of the rallies. But Serbian people is not demanding to be a leader but will not agree to be minor or second-rated. And then it goes on further below: We can say with pride that Muslims and Croats in the territory of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina are not in jeopardy and shall not be. Do you remember this was followed by applause? 50.000 people of Banja Luka supported this statement of mine with applause?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This quotation corresponds exactly to what I just said. I was not so precise, but I know that this was precisely the message sent to the Muslim and Croat people, of whom there was a significant number at the time in Banja Luka, and some of them were at this gathering, and these words you said were approved by an overwhelming majority of those present and most of them were Serbs who had come to greet the leading representatives of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From what you know, what was the position of Banja Luka's mayor towards Muslims and Croats? The mayor was Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radic testified in this case. We can find that information. But also from the documents we have here, we see that he constantly tried to protect the Muslim and Croat people, both, but primarily the Muslims, because the Croats enjoyed protection in some way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this does implicate some of the objections I was making earlier, but it's kind of squarely in front of us at the moment that we -- because the witness has repeatedly referred to his study of the documentation and so on. So now he directly refers in response to the question to documents he studied, evidence in this case, and I don't think there is any way of separating what this witness purports to have learned from his alleged study of certain documentation in the case and what he may or may not have known at the time, and if -- that may -- and probably is much more of a problem for Dr. Karadzic, but since it's consistent with the objection I've been making throughout, I thought I should make it known now. This -- and here we can see it as a particular problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you try to answer the question instead of giving your opinion? Do you understand the question? The question was the position of Mr. Radic at the time. You can answer the question as you remember, but you testify as if you were an expert after studying all the documents, you are giving your opinion. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just explain what my intention was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could just answer what the position of Mr. Radic was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of Mr. Radic, from the beginning to the end, was to protect the two ethnic communities and other non-Serbs, and I should like to be given a chance to explain why I testified as I did, if needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will take up that issue further, how; for example, how did you know that, et cetera. Shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you have personal experience of co-operation with Mr. Radic or did you find this out from documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my contacts with Mr. Radic, and also from talking to people who had more contact with him than I had, especially late Professor Koljevic, my opinion was that he was doing everything he could to protect the non-Serb population. And why did I refer to documents and evidence that appeared before? I'm not an expert, but I am aware, as Mr. Tieger said, he believes that I am a friend of Mr. Karadzic's and whatever I state cannot be credible enough unless I refer to some evidence. I wanted to tell the Trial Chamber not only then, during the war, but also during my trial, there appeared evidence that confirmed this view that Mr. Radic was protecting non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what attitude did Nebojsa Ivastanin, president of the Gradiska municipality, take towards Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as Mr. Radic. He made maximum efforts to protect non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we punish or otherwise disqualify Mr. Ivastanin, and what positions did he occupy after the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivastanin was appointed ambassador to Russia, I believe, after the war. He was part of the cadre that followed the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party, and that's how he was treated by the personnel policy of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik just said that Mr. Radic testified in this case. Was it the case? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a 92 quater submission, Mr. President. But it does beg the question in my mind of just how much information this witness has about the submissions in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we admitted pursuant to Rule 92 quater? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So his testimony in other case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, did you know that this was admitted into evidence? You said he testified. In which case did Mr. Radic testify?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was a witness who testified in public, in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that his evidence was admitted in my case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I didn't know about that document. I said Mr. Radic testified in my case, and I said that this confirmed what I had known before about the policy Mr. Radic pursued in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you about the attitude to Muslims and Croats and the policy of the SDS towards the other two ethnic communities, Latinovic, president of Dubica municipality; Luka Culic and Veljko Stupar from Mrkonjic Grad; the leadership of Drvar, Bosanska Grahovo, and Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milinic also testified in my case. But, regardless of that, I emphasise Mr. Milincic had the same position as Mr. Radic because Srbac was a majority Serbian place. And precisely in that area, as he confirmed before this Tribunal and as I had known before, that area called Kobas, I believe, contained some Croats who had stayed there, although they could have easily crossed the Sava River and gone to Croatia. As for Stupar in Mrkonjic Grad, when the Serbian forces came and took over Mrkonjic Grad, which was always Serbian, they were met by a great number of Muslims which -- who continued to live there until the end of the war. The situation was similar in the other areas you mentioned, where Serbs were in the majority, Croats were in the minority, and care was taken to pursue the policy dictated by the leadership of Republika Srpska, to provide maximum protection to minority populations, other ethnic communities who stayed in our areas and they were protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From what you knew at the time, did we ever voice objections against those presidents of municipalities and local authorities over the fact that they were taking good care of minority populations, or were we happy with them? What was our position towards their conduct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that always in various announcements and letters and documents are available here, we appealed on them to provide maximum security to the citizens from other ethnic communities. You can find the documents here but I know that we held a number of meetings at the time where the position was voiced to that effect, and as a leader of a party that was in power at the time, Mr. Karadzic, as the then-president, appealed on everyone and asked them to make sure that they protect not just the Geneva Conventions but also the customs which existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which traditionally preserved Bosnia-Herzegovina from unrest and conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber according to what you knew at the time, on what did it depend whether fighting would break out in a municipality and whether there would be conflict in a municipality, in some municipalities and not in others? Why in the 17 -- or, rather, 17 out of 27 Krajina municipalities they were -- there was fighting only in some of them in the valleys of Sana and Una, not in others where no one touched the Croats and the Muslims? Were these municipalities disobedient and did not implement our alleged genocidal policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert this, and you can find evidence about this, that all the conflicts that broke out, in the Sana river valley specifically, resulted from an initiative of the Muslim side. They initiated the conflict. Prijedor is an example. After this attack, and after many killed policemen, everything else that happened in the area followed. The initiators in these areas were unfortunately the militant circles and the militant individuals or groups, mostly Muslims but some Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now a little bit about the first months and the first year of the war. Could you tell us what the communication was like between the central republican organs in Pale and in Sarajevo and the organs in the local authorities, in the ground, primarily in the Krajina, to the west from the corridor, but also in other areas. And I mean all this in political terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now a little bit about the first months and first year of the war and soliciting information. If the Court thinks that is -- I mean, it's either an invitation for a very compendious answer by the witness tracking periods of time by periods of time, or it's too broad to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you could be more specific, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, the situation with regards to communication during the three years of war, was it always the same and what made it different and in what periods, if so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the same. Perhaps I might specify. Up until the 28th of June, 1992, all territorial links had been torn or they were very bad, I mean the land lines, especially close to Pale where the leadership was seated, the leadership of the Serbian Republic. After the month of June, when the corridor between the western and eastern parts of the republic was established, it was very risky to move through the area of Brcko, but there was some kind of territorial connection. Throughout 1992, I might say, the telephone and other communications, the similar ones like fax and printers, worked with lots of difficulties. And the conclusion which exists here, namely that because of this headquarters in Pale informations could reach it from various parts of Republika Srpska, I can explain that if you're interested, why the communication was not of the best quality, nor did we receive full or truthful information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of our system and in view of your experience, how did the municipalities operate in the former system and on our side during the war, especially during the first year? What kind of communication did we have and what was the influence of the central organs and how could this influence of the central organs be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To try to be as illustrative as possible, the municipalities were like small states within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not because they wanted to work in that way but because they were cut off and had no communications with any kind of centre and they were left to their own devices, and then the neighbouring municipalities sometimes linked together in order to resolve certain problems, especially with regard to defence and co-ordination, so that -- so that there was no important or major influence or instructions that were received from the central authorities, simply because due to difficulties in communication and general confusion and the state of war, this was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what you knew about the developments with regard to arrests of those who committed crimes and arrests of prisoners of war, what was happening on the ground, and how did you learn that this happened? Which prisons were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very rarely that you could receive truthful information about what was going on in the field. We were mostly preoccupied with what was happening to the Serbs in Sarajevo because that was closest to where we were, and in other areas from which we received alarming news about horrible crimes committed against the Serbian people. What was very rare, but it did happen, certain information that was unverified reached us and seemed more like a sort of report where someone is accusing somebody else of something. I claim that at our meetings, we never talked about reports that were unverified, and in which there were allusions to certain crimes without appropriate measures being taken. The relevant organs were charged with investigating it. It was always instructed that an investigation had to be carried out and the perpetrators punished. People were sent out to the ground to investigate. Instructions were sent out, too, and it happened like that throughout 1992. I knew that then and even though Mr. Prosecutor criticises me, I know that many such documents existed at the time. I was aware of many of them. I wasn't aware of others. They contained such instructions to people to do their work and act in accordance with their mandate. The greatest efforts to send such a message to the ground and to investigate those rumours were made by Mr. Karadzic, who was the president of the republic -- or, rather, the president of the Presidency, and he was the one who sent most such messages or he gave such messages or announcements to the media in his interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the interest for us and what kind of impact did the crimes that were happening on the ground have on us as the Serbian community, or any other misdemeanours on the ground? Did we order them? Did we tolerate them? And were they something that was to our advantage?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that whenever there was a report that may have been true, and where any allusion was made to a possible crime, then two institutions, first and foremost, the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please repeat. He's too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you were speaking too fast, Mr. Krajisnik. Could you repeat your answer after you said, "... first and foremost, the Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Justice, and the army, the military. As far as I remember, there were other separate commissions but these were the three main institutions which were given the task to investigate the issues, to establish the truth, and to punish the perpetrators. Every meeting that I attended ended with such a conclusion being adopted. In the parliament as well, there was report about something, then a conclusion was adopted, and instructions were given to these institutions to investigate this and establish it because they were the only ones who were in charge of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the Presidency and the assembly or the government, these three highest organs of power, did they have their own investigative institutions? And in what manner could they -- who -- or who could they order to investigate this? Or did they have their own organs that could carry out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency did not have at its disposal any instruments of investigation. The same for the assembly. The government had two ministries that could implement this. There were individual cases, too, when someone would be assigned to investigate this but the only regular avenue was through these three institutions. Of course, also the Prosecutor's office, and so on. But I'm talking about those who were within the government and could verify the truth about certain allegations that we received as reports or information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If these organs and the courts did their work, did the assembly or the Presidency have any impact on the outcome of these processes? Did they meddle with this, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody outside the government or outside these institutions could have any influence on it. I couldn't influence someone to implement or not implement something. I could ask them, I could wish, or I don't know what else, I could send a letter or a conclusion from the assembly but I couldn't order anything. I can just provide an example where I received an objection from a lady who had been expelled from her apartment in the Zvornik municipality. I sent my personal secretary to establish this and to try to help this unfortunate woman who found herself out in the street with her children. The then-president -- the then-assembly speaker said, Why did Krajisnik do this? We liberated this. We are in power here. What does Krajisnik want to do with it? My secretary returned and said, Let's punish him. How should we do it? Tell me, I asked him, we can help this woman. This one protected witness testified here about this, and this is an example that I know well. It happened to me in my case. And certainly at the level of the Presidency, there were similar cases but they couldn't do it without the instruments of power which I listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who appointed the judges in our judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly of Republika Srpska -- or, rather, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the proposal of the government -- or, rather, the Ministry of Justice appointed the judges, in the civilian and in the military courts. But in case of military judges and military prosecutors, it was not a proposal of the government but I think it was the proposal of the Ministry of Defence, as far as I know. That was normal. I suppose that there was also a suggestion of the Main Staff. I don't know this exactly, but I know that both kinds of judges and prosecutors were appointed by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when the assembly could not meet for an assembly session, who would then appoint the judges up until their nomination was confirmed by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency did, the then-Presidency, but the assembly had to confirm the decision later on because it was not final until the assembly adopted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any instances in which the Presidency or the assembly, the Presidency at the time, imposed some judges or removed the judges from the list when it intervened with the proposal of the ministry and the government? Do you know of any such instances of the Presidency intervening with the ministry's proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such proposals but there were proposals to the effect that the assembly rejected the proposal of the Presidency -- rather, the decision, not the proposal, but the decision of the Presidency, so it was not upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly explain or clarify what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an example of an instance when the Presidency appointed the judges and prosecutors who were Muslims by ethnicity and that between two assembly sessions when the assembly could not convene, the Presidency accepted that and made the decision, and then it was published in the Official Gazette. And then consequently at one of the assembly sessions, the decision was not rescinded but there was no support for it. It was not supported. That's one example. Perhaps there may have been others when it had to do with the Serbs but this was a drastic example, when the Muslim judges and the Muslim and Croatian prosecutors were at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it a permanent tendency in the assembly and what was given as the reason? What made the MPs request a different solution?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, this was done in a sort of vacuum. The MPs did not have anything against appointing the Muslims and the Croats as judges and prosecutors but as this was a period when we had a crisis in the negotiations, a crisis on the ground, when fierce war was being waged and there was awful propaganda from, conditionally speaking, the other side, then the MPs were revolted and they stood up against such a decision. Not because they would reject it permanently but they said that the time was not ripe, that because there was war going on and there were hostilities and the other side would not allow the Serbs to leave, they were being maltreated and killed, and on this side, that is to say the Serbian side, people would be awarded even though they belonged to another ethnicity. And then the then-minister of justice, Mr. Mandic, fought vehemently against freezing this decision. And as far as I remember, Mr. Karadzic tried on several occasions to explain to the MPs and presented to them as a good message to the world, but the MPs who were overwhelmed by emotion because of the day-to-day politics and the war and the situation on the other side did not agree with this. But in order to understand rightly this decision, we should take into account that that was, I think, on the 11th or the 12th of August, and before that, perhaps a month or fortnight earlier, there was an assembly session in Pale, that was the second assembly session held after the outbreak of the war, and there were many hard words which were said with regards to irregularities, crime and so on, and this was the continuation of the session. And on the previous day, the MP club met, Mr. Karadzic was not present, and I fought a hard battle with the MPs trying to persuade them to accept this. And they voiced their arguments. And eventually the conclusion was, Okay, let's not do it now. We'll do it later. That's why at the assembly session itself, Mr. Karadzic, once he arrived, he did not know that we had had that discussion on the previous day and that we had made this agreement. And so I said, No one has anything against those Muslims. On the contrary, however. Please this is not the right time. Let's try to postpone it, so as to preserve the cohesion within the assembly because it was on the edge of a rift because people did not want to pursue any policy. They were just thinking how they needed to say what they were feeling at the time and the emotions are rarely a good ally of wise decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the position was of the leadership in respect of humanitarian and civilian needs of the population of the other two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Nikola Koljevic, as a top official of Republika Srpska, as a member of the Presidency, was appointed by the Presidency to take care of a particular way of helping the Muslim and Croat people by way of making sure that the convoys passed unhindered with humanitarian aid, that is. I know that there are many documents showing what a battle the Presidency headed by Mr. Karadzic waged in order to have this humanitarian aid reach these enclaves. Very often, there were even conflicts, verbal conflicts, between the military structures and the civilian authorities. Because the soldiers, in the view of the civilian authorities, in a way, obstructed the convoys from reaching a particular destination, sometimes. However, the explanation provided by the military was that through humanitarian aid, arms were being smuggled in and other impermissible things. It was really a disaster when that was proven to be true. In some humanitarian convoys, there were weapons that were being smuggled in. Regardless of that, I know, I heard that, I was present, when Mr. Karadzic said, When, for example, an international community member would come to, as a soldier you have to be correct, also to those who are escorting convoys because we should never fight against our enemy in that way because that was never part of the nature of our people and our army. That is my experience. That is my knowledge. And it is easy for you, Judges, to establish that on the basis of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you briefly to speak about military developments in Sarajevo itself. How far away is Pale from Sarajevo? And from a military point of view, how was Sarajevo structured? The lines, the neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With small corrections, Judges, at the beginning of the war, every ethnic community stood in its own ethnic areas. The configuration of Sarajevo, if you look at the inner city, is populated by Muslims, and the periphery, that is to say everything outside the city, are Serb ethnic areas. Most of the Muslims were in town, and also the government was Muslim. In that area, they had a large army of soldiers who, according to the information that we received from our army, very often attacked the areas that were held by our army, that is to say our fighters. Further away from this inner city, these small towns, like part of Vogosca, Ilijas, Rajlovac, all of that was Serb, and they were surrounded by Muslims. There were Muslim sieges there. An expert could tell you about that. But the density of population was less there so then there were these two rings, if I can put it that way. Everybody felt threatened, Serbs by the Muslims from Visoko towards Sarajevo, and Muslims from the Serbs in the urban centre of town. This was this front between the two ethnic communities, although the third ethnic community was a bit further away. So in essence, the ethnic areas made this necessary. You were there, you saw this. There was this border between the Muslim and Serb ethnic parts. It looks as if somebody had blocked someone. However, our soldiers, the representatives of our Main Staff, said that there were at least 30 offensives launched by the Muslims so that they would break through this defence line of the Serb army. I mean, during the war, there were 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At a political level, did we have orders to take Muslim parts of Sarajevo in military terms? Actually, what was our position towards the Muslim-held parts of town?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have such a plan. And I'm telling you, as I testified a moment ago, several times foreigners and our soldiers were of the opinion that with the Army of Republika Srpska we could have taken Sarajevo. However, the main protagonist, and the main opponent of taking Sarajevo was precisely Mr. Karadzic, the president. He said several times that that would have been a terrible mistake, that there would have been many casualties, many fatalities, and it would have been a crime against the civilian population and it would be very hard to carry out this kind of operation without a lot of civilian casualties. Also, the policy was not to take Sarajevo but rather to transform Sarajevo into two towns, along with a small Croat municipality where every ethnic community would have its own government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the break, just one more question: What was our position vis-a-vis operations in town? The information that we received from the foreign factor, the media, about sniping, about artillery operations against town, was that accurate? Was that correct? And what was our position in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was the most difficult problem for the Serb side because many Serbs were in captivity in Sarajevo. No one was allowed to leave freely. Many had to pay bribes in order to get out, and people had to ask for favours in order to get out of Sarajevo. So this was terrible pressure in terms of our leadership and the military. How to help people. No one knew how to help them. The army that was in Sarajevo very often, very often, provoked our army. They would hit them in order to elicit a response, if I can put it that way. This was based on a political decision, I mean the Muslim and Croat side, or rather the Muslim side in this situation. They wanted to represent Sarajevo as a victim and to represent us, our army, as an aggressor, people who were attacking in order to take a territory. I can give you an example. From my family, two women who were at home were killed by sniper. My wife was a victim of the shelling of Sarajevo. My uncle also died. My cousin was killed by a sniper, a woman. And there were many such cases. There were women who were killed in the place where I lived until the end of this war, where I lived during the war and after that. Now I'm a refugee at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you suggest a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. One question you didn't answer is the distance between Pale and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 30 and 20 kilometres. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, less probably. I cannot say but it's not very far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When I asked you, Mr. Speaker, about our position concerning humanitarian aid, could you actually give us an expanded answer -- or, no, you did answer it, in terms of allowing them. Actually, what was our position vis-a-vis the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, the UNHCR? Do you remember our positions? Do you remember our documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as the beginning of the war, there was this meeting at Ilidza attended by Mr. Cutileiro I think, as far as I can remember, and then there were other people there too. As regards all international humanitarian organisations, our side had a favourable attitude. We appealed to our citizens asking them to honour their function. The leadership had many meetings, supporting their activities, and the leadership was forthcoming, in terms of allowing their activity to go on unhindered, along with a great deal of help from us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at 1D65260 in e-court? At the 11th of December, 1992, I think -- this is something different, 1D65260. This has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this? This is an agreement, a recommendation on the tragic situation of civilians in Bosnia-Herzegovina signed by Trnka, Kalinic, Coric, Kurjak, Popadic, Mujic. Do you remember these documents that were signed regulating the question of providing assistance to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this agreement. It wasn't only this one. There were many other agreements. I think that there was one actually before this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the agreement of the 22nd of May, 1992, that was signed by Kalinic on our behalf, and do you remember what this agreement regulated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know the date concerned but I know that there was an agreement that regulated activities of the International Red Cross. Mr. Kalinic, the then-minister of health and social policy signed that agreement on your behalf with the representatives of -- I think it was exactly these representatives that I see here. I know Mr. Kurjak was there, I think it was Mr. Trnka, but I don't know exactly whether all of those people listed here were there. But I remember this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I make a mistake or is there another agreement of the 11th of December?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karadzic, if you see the last page, it's dated as 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably in that document, that document of the 11th is probably there too. Since the witness knows about this, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in respect of -- in respect of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, has this been admitted? Is there a P -- no, a D document? No. Could we have the first page yet again, please? Could we see the bottom of the page too? This was at the invitation of the Red Cross, the 30th of September and the 1st of October are the dates when it was signed. I believe this must have been admitted. Could we have the last page again? D1141. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at number 5? [In English] Areas of origin should benefit as vulnerable group from international assistance, inter alia in conformity with its mandate by the ICRC. [Interpretation] What was our position in respect of the population that had been temporarily transferred? Was our position that this was supposed to go on forever on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The damage is done and we know the impact on the probative value of any answers elicited, but I will have to continue making these objections apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D1141 seems to be the correct one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, what was our official and private position vis-a-vis persons who were displaced from their home towns and villages during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as expressed in paragraph 5 of this agreement, and as indicated later in many communiques coming from the officials of the ICRC, namely that certain vulnerable groups may be allowed to leave for safer areas with the proviso that it cannot be regarded as ethnic cleansing or their permanent displacement from their home areas where they must have the right to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the indictment, it says that it was my objective, and the JCE objective, to permanently remove Croats from the territories which we claimed as ours. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, this is completely untrue. There was not a single decision, a position taken, or a document issued that advocated such a policy. I am convinced of that, unless somebody perhaps interprets things differently or an individual makes an unauthorised statement otherwise. Our position was exactly as the position expressed by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this has been admitted into evidence, it can be removed. Let us come back to the issue of Sarajevo. What did the army explain to us in reply to allegations that they were firing at the city?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we asked representatives of the army, the explanation we got was that there had been an attack launched from Sarajevo first, in the form of an infantry attack or infantry fire to break through the lines of the Serbian army, and that would happen when a protest was made by some representative of the international community because we had not been notified about such things before. We had not been notified in advance by those who made the accusations that disproportionate force was used by our army. So these were attempts to break through our lines, the lines of our army, and our army could not respond in a different way because their personnel was ten times less numerous than the enemy. They could only respond with artillery to the fire coming from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You talked about sabotage actions in Sarajevo and attempts to win outside sympathy. What do you know about the explosion in the Vasa Miskin Crni Street, Markale I and II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we get there, Mr. Krajisnik you just answered that "... our army could not respond in a different way ..." Could you expand on that? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two types of response by our army. In the city, there was a great infantry force, and the Muslim infantry attacked our areas where our defence lines were stretched thin and undermanned, and the only way was to strike against that greater power coming from the city. But much more often there was artillery fire from certain points in the city, and then our army responded against those areas where the fire originated. Those were the two responses we usually got. And there was no other response. And I can refer you to a telephone conversation between Mr. Abdic and Colonel Gagovic from our barracks. So they are talking and Abdic is defending himself saying that the army is attacking certain neighbourhoods in the city and Mr. Gagovic says, But your people are attacking us from your area and I already have three soldiers killed by your artillery. There are more such examples where the army responded to fire that originated from the city so that somebody would end up killed. Those were the only two explanations, justifications, for the fighting inside the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember there was one question; namely, what do you know about incidents involving mass losses of civilian life in Sarajevo? Let me remind you 27 May 1992, Vasa Miskin Crni Street; then February 1994, the incident in Dobrinja, that was 4th February; and the 5th of February, Markale I; and in end August 1995, Markale II. What do you know about these massively lethal incidents? And do you know of any other similar incidents that are undoubtedly provoked by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you about one thing. I was very often at the airport, together with Haris Silajdzic, accompanied by several people from their side and several from our side and some representatives of the international community. We were trying to come to some agreement to calm down the situation in the city. And very often Silajdzic would say, There has been an incident. I have to leave. And some of these incidents were those you just mentioned. And I remember very well the follow-up activities. There would be a complaint, a protest, then a response from the international community, and our army would immediately respond that the shell had not come from our area. Then our leadership, primarily Mr. Karadzic, insisted on an immediate investigation to find out what exactly happened because we had very strong assurances from the representatives of the Main Staff, Mr. Mladic or somebody else, that it could not possibly be a Serbian shell and that an inquiry needs to be made. Unfortunately, reports would follow rejecting our initiative to conduct an inquiry. It all ended with half-finished steps wherein we would be denying that it was our side, the Muslims would be insisting that it was, and the international reports would be divided, some saying that it might be, others that it couldn't have been. It's a great pity that the truth was never established because other operations and other incidents followed with a persisting accusation that it was caused by our side. Truth was needed not only to establish responsibility but to resolve this status quo in which it was our word against theirs. There was also the warning, oft repeated by Mr. Karadzic, that the army must not attack Sarajevo because that would be used as a pretext to attack our army with air strikes. As I said, unfortunately, the investigation was never completed and doubts remain to this day. One such incident was used to get our artillery to withdraw, and that was the main deterrent for the Muslims to refrain from attacking our positions. So later, they did attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just now you said Mr. Karadzic issued an order that army must not attack Sarajevo. Is it consistent with your previous answer that you -- the army could not respond in a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is consistent. Talking to soldiers -- although I didn't have many such meetings, soldiers were often told how detrimental to us the accusations that we were attacking Sarajevo were. And Mr. Karadzic reacted by saying that even if you are attacked, it has to be proven that you had been attacked first because very often nobody knows who started first, and these accusations are hurting us seriously. The other side persisted in the propaganda, accusing us for things for which we were not to blame. What is certain is that our policy was not attack Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was regarding the earlier issue on page 70 or 71. What explanations did the army give us concerning their fire? What kind of response were you talking about? The military response or the response to our questions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of the army gave us a clear answer, that they were responding to attacks from the city, that they were responding against the neighbourhoods from which fire was opened at the army. That was their explanation for certain army activities. And you, and the leadership, told them that it has to be shown clearly to the international community that the initial attack really happened before our army reacted, instead of justifying ourselves after the fact. So when you asked them, Are these allegations that I heard from the international community true, these are the explanations they gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were on the 27th of May, the day of the explosion in Vasa Miskin Street and what did we do and conclude in that respect, and what kind of answer did we get from the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you an example a moment ago. I believe that's precisely that example, although it might have been another incident. But I still believe it's this one. A protest was made, you were informed that the shell had landed there, killing a lot of people, you were informed by some international representatives, and then when you contacted the army, the army clearly said, This is not our shell. After receiving that answer, you immediately sent out a demand to conduct an inquiry involving a ballistics expert to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you know about the other incidents, primarily Markale I and II and several shellings in Dobrinja resulting in great loss of life?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same procedure, the same situation as in that first incident. Our military said that it was a frame-up, that it was not our shell, and, Your Honours, what was important was that all these incidents resembled closely incidents in other countries. So it was easy to portray this by saying, you know, this is the same policy as in Beirut, Sarajevo is very much like it, and the explanations we got from our military were always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who benefited politically from these incidents that we disputed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was absolutely to the detriment of the Serbian side and to the benefit of the militant circles in Sarajevo. I'm talking only about the militant circles in Sarajevo who wanted to portray Sarajevo as a martyr, as a prison, as a victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to touch upon the issue of the paramilitaries. What was my position and the position of the leadership, regarding armed individuals and groups, that is to say paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of Republika Srpska, and also the commander of the Main Staff, were completely opposed to volunteer units that were outside of control and which we christened as paramilitary formations because they were not under anyone's command. Many times it was stated, both by soldiers and directly by Mr. Mladic, that he criticised any wilfulness that appeared, and I clearly said that all soldiers who want to fight for us can do so but under the command of our army, and those who didn't want to do so would have to return from where they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did our side prohibit the paramilitaries and arrest them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many instances in which, from your part, you sent an order and so did the Main Staff, to the effect that specific paramilitary formations be disarmed and expelled. Some were disarmed and expelled, and others accepted to come under the command of our units and thus joined them. Therefore, there was a very strict order to the effect that no paramilitary formations should exist. When we received reports about units which were out of control, an order would follow for it to be eliminated, and there are such examples among your documents with orders coming from the Supreme Commander, that is to say Mr. Karadzic, who issued such orders on behalf of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us which state was in existence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yugoslavia still existed on the 31st of March and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a federal unit. Republika Srpska did not exist as an internationally recognised entity, even though by the 31st of March, namely on the 9th of January, we proclaimed Republika Srpska as our response and the expression of our political position. But at the time Republika Srpska did not officially exist. There were still the official organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that the interpreters missed the date. I was asking you about the 31st of March, 1992. Do you know, and what do you know about the events in Bijeljina? Did anyone from our side invite Arkan and his fighters to Bijeljina, and in what capacity did Ms. Plavsic travel to Bijeljina during that crisis?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, I remember the date well, actually I remember the events which had to do with Bijeljina. I was in the office of the parliament speaker of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ms. Plavsic, I think Mr. Jerko Doko, Mr. Abdic and I think Mr. Zepinic, or whoever else, were there as a delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They went to Bijeljina. It wasn't Ms. Plavsic who was there -- she wasn't there as a representative of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Arkan was invited and was present and fought in Republika Srpska in that period between April 1992 and September or October 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have forgotten to say that none of the authorities in Republika Srpska invited Arkan. He came to Bijeljina at a local initiative on the basis of a local invitation, when the fighting had already ended or almost ended. Now, whether Arkan was present in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were some units, some paramilitary formations or groups which claimed that they were Red Berets, something similar to Arkan, but Arkan was not present in Republika Srpska. It was those units that created this image that could help to establish a link with Arkan, but I think that Arkan was not present in Republika Srpska almost until the end of the war, or at least I'm not aware of his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 102 of the pre-trial brief claims that in the evening on the 31st of March, 1992, the Serb volunteer guard, that is to say the Arkan's men and the local Territorial Defence forces, attacked Bijeljina, killed at least 48 Muslim civilians and took over the power in this town. First of all, did the crisis break out after Arkan's arrival or did Arkan arrive after the crisis broke out? And who was in power in Bijeljina before and after this? And were all the killed persons Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, as I just said, Arkan did not come when the fighting broke out, nor did he participate in the fighting while the fighting lasted. He came near the end or after the fighting had ceased. I'm not quite certain about that. What is true about it is that this incident was provoked by the militant circles and militant groups among the Muslims in Bijeljina. A conflict did break out and then, if I may put it so, the local forces were more powerful. Arkan arrived and he was involved in the final operations or perhaps he got there after the end of the incident. The absolute power in Bijeljina, up until the incident, was held by the Serbian side, so that the definition or the conclusion that the Serbian side took over the power was wrong. It had no reason to do it because it held the power in Bijeljina before that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember why Bijeljina reacted so vehemently? Was there anything that happened before that in Bosnia-Herzegovina which made them react so vehemently?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and evidence corroborates it. There were two serious incidents in Kupres and in Sijekovac, near Bosanski Brod, wherein in one place it was the Croatian forces and in the other the Muslim forces that attacked on Serbian civilians and committed a crime. And in the chain of events which followed one another, this was a third incident in which once again militant individuals and groups wanted to seize power in Bijeljina. They attacked Serbian civilians, or actually Serbian citizens, which sent a powerful warning to Bijeljina which then defended itself from those men who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please remember the war commissioners; that is to say, what were the various ways in which the central authorities were trying to exert their influence on the municipalities? Why did war commissioners exist and what was their role?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Djukanovic, the president of a minor political party before the war, the party of federalists, who advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia and that Bosnia should stay in Yugoslavia, came to Pale at the invitation of the late Nikola Koljevic and held talks with you and Mr. Koljevic and proposed that as the local authorities could not operate and as we had no contact with various locations on the ground, to establish commissioners, the commissioners of the Presidency, who would then make tours of the ground and to try to help with establishing powers, establishing authorities, because there were practically no authorities that were operating at the time. They were let me call them Crisis Staffs or the like. Everyone was trying to establish something that would work in one way or another. So as it was the time of war already, these were war commissioners, that was how they were called and then I think they had a different title, there was another one, but decisions followed one another. The task of these commissioners was to go out into the field, to try to see what the situation was like, and help the local population and the local authorities to establish regular, lawful authorities rather than to have Crisis Staffs or some other ad hoc groups. The goal was to establish authorities and power on the ground in that way. Because up until that time, there were no authorities at all, or we received all sorts of unverified reports. We were not sure about the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of the paragraphs from the introduction to the pre-trial brief, under item 7, it is said that Mladic and myself and others formulated and implemented the plan to take UN staff as hostages in order to prevent air strikes against the military targets of the Bosnian Serbs. And it says there those air strikes represented a threat to the military capacities of the Bosnian Serbs, and the ability of Bosnian Serb leaderships to achieve their military and political goals. Mr. Speaker, do you remember whether we agreed to the mandate and the military presence of the UN, and could they be present there without our consent in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of the international community, that was the UNPROFOR at the time, were welcome so that they would help us to reach some sort of solution. Without our consent it would have been very difficult to achieve that at the time. We had good co-operation with UNPROFOR. But at one point, due to the instances that I mentioned, such as Markale and attacks, there was this constant threat to our side that we would be bombed. And we received information that the other side saw the only way out in which they would achieve their goals to have UNPROFOR on its side so that they would bomb Serbian targets and help them to defeat Serbs in such a way. There was a constant activity in order to avoid those threats of air strikes, but outside of any mandate, there was this threat that Serbian positions would be bombed. We considered this to be UNPROFOR taking side with one of the warring parties, which was beyond its mandate at the time. The way I saw this stage, when this thing with UNPROFOR soldiers happened, it was a desperate attempt on part of our army to prevent further air strikes because it was so difficult when towns and infrastructure are being destroyed. It was in no case a wish to harm those young men who were shown on TV. If it was also an intention to deter further air strikes, that was why we showed it on TV. We wanted to deter someone from exposing us to air strikes. We had no wish to destroy these young people. I saw an aircraft going down above Pale and how the locals in Pale held these two or three young men who had been taken prisoner. They treated them as their own children. So in my view, though I must stress I'm a layman and not a soldier, the image that was sent to the public was one of deterrent with the aim of ending the air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that they were taken prisoner in accordance with a plan which Mladic, myself and others formulated to take UN personnel as hostages. Did we ask the United Nations not to meddle in the war, not to be involved, and did we inform them that if they did so that they would be treated as enemies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There are a number of statements in which we warned that the UNPROFOR and international community representatives should not meddle. Here is my example: The air strikes at Pale, which is 10 to 15 kilometres away, perhaps ten kilometres as the crow flies, it was bombed, and my wife was a victim, and we received information that UNPROFOR was helping in air strikes on Pale, actually. I don't know if this is true, but the Muslim side did not have such power and such artillery because the distance is quite big, so Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic very often warned the UNPROFOR representatives, or the international community representatives, that they should not meddle in the conflict but help for the conflict to be overcome or that unless they did so they would be considered enemies. Documents to this effect exist and this can be easily checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember until what time the Muslim armed forces existed in Podrinje, from the area south of Zvornik down to Zepa and Srebrenica including Konjevic Polje and this entire area? Up until when did they exist and could the situation in Podrinje be resolved without any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. I think that it was up until the end of the war, in fact, or almost. The entire area was occupied by the Muslim forces, I don't remember the exact date, but almost until the end of the war, or close by that time. It was a dappled area, parts of which were occupied by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the Cerska affair and what the media reported about our counter-offensive against Cerska? How was it characterised and how did General Morillon go there to check it? Were you aware of that? You didn't have to be, but were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of our people were involved in the war so I was following developments too. Some information arrived to the effect that genocide had been committed in Cerska, that many people were killed. A good French general, Mr. Morillon, arrived and went there to see where it was that genocide had been committed. He went to Srebrenica, and from there he tried to check whether something like that had happened, if that is the case involved. I think it is. Then he was a kind of hostage there because the Muslim forces would not allow him to leave, and he stated then that what the propaganda said was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your experience with such media fire works, or, rather, this kind of media representation of certain events? To what extent could that be believed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The worst was when you knew about something that had happened, and in the media you see that even the representatives of the international community who had been misled are providing information that is the complete opposite. Then you get a confirmation or, rather, a conviction that other similar information that you had received is of that same nature. There was a lot of information like that. You'd watch television and you'd see the revolt of the people and everyone about this, how this propaganda - how do I put this? - was being used to attain somebody's objectives. For instance, we saw this well-known journalist from a respectable media company, on a particular TV programme. He showed a cemetery with many crosses and he says, Look, look at how many Muslims the Serbs had killed. And only we there know how tombstones are marked in that part of the world at various cemeteries. I'm not blaming anyone but there was a lot of propaganda at the time during the war, and lies became astronomical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say how incidents in Sarajevo were treated by the media and how incidents -- or, rather, events concerning Srebrenica were treated in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe I will be imprecise because it's hard to be precise. Everybody in the war had their own truth. All the media presented things that happened in a certain way. Muslims - I mean, I'm talking about Muslims in Sarajevo. The Croats were a bit further away so it's hard for me to speak in the plural, therefore, so I'm speaking in the singular, so I'm talking about the army and the people belonging to one ethnic group - they always presented things in a very abrasive way, that they were the victims, that the Serbs were the aggressors attacking and so on. As for Srebrenica, I can just say the following: As far as our side is concerned, no matter who I contacted and that goes for the media too, things were portrayed as Srebrenica being liberated because there was no resistance and this was quite a bit of surprise. And this was a sort of positive thing because before that, we had a lot of failures in the west, in the western parts, so this led to a certain relaxation among the people, or perhaps the better way of putting it is satisfaction. This was portrayed as a victory that one should be happy about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember now in the media, and also in letters written by foreigners, what was stated -- what happened in Srebrenica? Who were the victims in Srebrenica during those days? And could this be believed or trusted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the media on the Serb side - that's what I do know - it was presented in the following way: That the Muslim army, before our army even arrived, started its breakthrough towards Tuzla, and that even Zvornik was in jeopardy. They even could have taken that. And during this breakthrough, there had been quite a few casualties. There was no information whatsoever about the killing of any person or rather that a crime had been committed there. If someone would even ask what happened there, they would always say, They are lying, that's not true. That is roughly what I can remember, given this time distance, what it was like in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether at the time there was any mention of killing of prisoners of war near Srebrenica, or was it being stated for a long time that in Srebrenica itself, thousands of civilians had been killed, rather boys and men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. The witness stated in his previous answer what he could remember, now he's asked for what he -- again what he could remember, and he's being provided helpful, or potentially helpful, details about what he might or might not remember. Let's find out what he remembers, if he's being asked that, rather than guiding the answer in any way. I don't see the need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In his previous answer he mentioned primarily what he heard from the Serb side. So we can ask him whether he heard any mention of killing of prisoners of war. Can you answer the question, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for certain information from the representatives of the international community, there was some. Even then it was not being said that people had been killed or that there had been an execution. In a way, it was being said as if the Serb forces had taken a safe area without authorisation, and in that respect a certain precedent had occurred or, rather, something impermissible had happened. And of course in that fighting it was stated that there were some people who had lost their lives. However, for a long time, even foreigners did not say -- I mean, international representatives did not speak about any kind of execution. I did not hear from a single foreigner at the time that there was an execution. I did not hear about that at that time. And I think that the representatives of the Serbs did not say to anyone that there had been such an execution during those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If not execution, could you be more specific as to what you heard from the representatives of international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for what I heard, it was being stated that the Serb side had taken a safe area and that there were a lot of refugees and there were images of civilians that were being shown and it was being stated that there was a looming humanitarian catastrophe. And nobody talked about the soldiers who were attempting a breakthrough, or there was no reference to any execution. There was more talk about how these refugees would be taken care of, how the situation in Srebrenica would be normalised, and also there was concern and also there was a threat that Republika Srpska could be bombed because of the taking of Srebrenica. As for crimes, I did not hear about that from the representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, according to the diaries of my secretaries, we met a few times during those days, mainly in the presence of other people, various delegations. Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. It was as much a cautionary rising as much, but I mean obviously the accused was about -- was in the process of providing the witness with information that's evidence in this case concerning the question he's going to ask. I don't mind the question going forward at this point, but I was certainly concerned about the continuation of the provision of information before seeking whatever evidence this witness might purport to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be cautious not to put a leading question, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P2242. Perhaps we can call that up. And then the pages that have to do with the 13th, the 15th, the 18th, the 19th of July. During those days did you see me in my office? Did we meet in my office? And do you remember what the topics were and what the need was for us to meet at the time? If you see who else was there, perhaps that might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The month of July, please. The 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 91?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this here, Minister Rosic, Minister Pejic, Kapetina, President Krajisnik and Petra Markovic, Milorad Motika, and Colonel Orasanin on the 13th. Do you remember? And what would these names tell you? What was the topic that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given this time distance, I cannot remember the details of these meetings. I can just interpret that which is logical. On the 13th and on the 14th, as for the people who are listed here, these were the usual kind of meetings held with different people. Perhaps we could find such meetings on many dates before and after. As far as I can see here, Krajisnik, Bulatovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, the 14th -- no, the 13th, please. On the left. On the right, can you tell us about Kapetina, Pejic, Petra Markovic, Milorad Motika, and Colonel Orasanin. What is it that they deal with? If that was that meeting, what was the topic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find that. If we are talking about the 13th I cannot find my name, so I'd like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the handwritten part?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, Rosic, yes, as far as I can remember, he was minister of justice; Minister Pejic was minister of finance; Kapetina was the deputy or assistant minister of defence; I was the speaker of the assembly; Petra Markovic was -- was in finance. Actually, perhaps Mr. Pejic was not minister of finance at the time. He was in charge of the building of the city of Sarajevo. Petra Markovic was minister of finance. Actually, Milorad Motika and Colonel Orasanin, they were officials from ORAO, a company. So all of this probably had to do with the town of Sarajevo. I really have no other explanation. This meeting, it's quite diverse, if I can put it that way, and it really has nothing to do with the subject matter that we are discussing now. I mean, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Motika and Orasanin, do they come from Pretis and ORAO? And what about these people from finance, why are they there with them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Motika was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know how many times this witness has to say he doesn't remember this meeting and that it has -- and all that he considers the number of participants to have a kind diverse background. But the accused persists in trying to elicit from him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness said they were from ORAO, a company, and I take it Mr. Karadzic was trying to clarify what that meant when he said Pretis. Shall we continue? Please continue, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Excellency, because ORAO doesn't mean a thing to someone who doesn't know that this is a factory that makes aircraft engines. Pretis and ORAO, both, but all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time, between quarter to 7.00 and 9.30, was there any mention, a single word, regarding Srebrenica and crimes in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that at that meeting, at that time, in my presence, no one spoke about what happened in Srebrenica and that is why I claim that at this meeting, there was no such discussion because I certainly would have remembered that. Now, why am I in a position to interpret this? Perhaps Mr. Tieger will be sorry to hear this but just like in other trials, witnesses interpreted somebody's speech. I can say with a great deal of certainty what could have happened at this meeting. This meeting could only discuss the protection of Sarajevo because there were large-scale offensives against Sarajevo at the time, so with a view to protecting the people there. So it was with a great deal of certainty that I can say that these people could have discussed that only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to this same diary - and if it's necessary we can take a look at this - you came to see me on the 15th, 18th and 19th of July. I believe that it was always as part of some group.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see the 14th here. Can you see that? Line 4, there is Deronjic, and the delegation of Srebrenica, from 14.25 to 18.25. At the time, were you present? Or did you go to a press conference? I thought I saw that somewhere. Ah, yes. President Krajisnik says -- just a moment, please. From 14.10 to 16.15, do you remember that? It's down here. Yes. Yes. It's right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you heard about the format of this diary, Mr. Krajisnik, who wrote this and in what method she was keeping this diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All our secretaries noted down all the parties that came to call on us in their own way. I found out later, because originally I didn't know about there agenda, the secretary of Mr. Karadzic noted this down and I have no reason to doubt it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You heard this. Do you see your name in the middle of 14th, President Krajisnik, 14.10 to 16.15 hours? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you see a plus in front of your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When there is an appointment it will be just a minus, when the people shows up then it will turn into a plus. Do you understand that? So it shows that you met president at 14.10. Do you agree so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
