utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that I don't know whether it works that way. I suppose so. But I really have no recollection whatsoever of this meeting. It might have happened. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's in our evidence. So if you see -- how many -- four lines above your entry, you see Miroslav Deronjic. Probably he was -- he had an appointment at 11.00 hours but probably -- but he showed up as a delegate at 14.25 while you are meeting Mr. Karadzic. So Miroslav Deronjic and a delegation from Srebrenica met Karadzic from 1.425 to 16.25. So while you are meeting with president, I take it this delegation arrived. Do you remember such incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat: I don't remember the meeting. But looking at this, Milos Culafovic was there at the time, at two different times, and I see Mrs. Tereza Guld was received by Krajisnik. It's possible that I spent some brief time with Mr. Culafovic, maybe it's the same time as I met briefly with Karadzic, or maybe I left to attend another meeting in the middle of this, but I saw a recording showing Mr. Deronjic and his delegation with Karadzic, and I don't remember that at all. But if the recording shows me there, that must have been -- then I must have been at that meeting with Karadzic, Deronjic and the delegation. I don't know how long, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ver well. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look, please, Bob Djurdjevic was there from 17.00 hours until 19.15. That means that he was there for an hour and a half at the same time as Miroslav Deronjic. Did Bob Djurdjevic sit in the same room as the delegation of Srebrenica? In other words, can you remember all the rooms where activities took place in the building of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of the Presidency, there were several offices and auxiliary offices where various talks intertwined, all combinations were possible. It's possible that I first met with Culafovic, and then I briefly left to see Deronjic, and then I joined another meeting, and then somebody would move to a different office, so Mr. Karadzic would leave a meeting for a while to receive somebody else. All these combinations are possible. I cannot claim anything with any certainty now. I can just look at the same paper as you are looking at and reflect on all the possibilities. What is certain is that it very often happened that somebody would come in the middle of a meeting we had, one of us would temporarily leave the meeting, receive that person in another room, then rejoin the meeting, and sometimes they would end up joining the meeting again when it was almost over. So everything is possible. I can only tell you general things that may be of use to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 14th, was there any talk with me, with Deronjic, with people from Skelani and Srebrenica? Was there any talk about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was at that meeting, as the footage shows me, I can only say that nobody talked about any negative aspect of the events in Srebrenica, in my presence. I remember there was no talk of any crimes. No matter what evidence is produced, I am absolutely sure there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the entry for the 15th, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see it in e-court. [In English] Next page, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, there is a minus next to Stoltenberg's name. He had announced himself and didn't come. Drago Simic, the same. It says call President Krajisnik, plus. And then a meeting, President Krajisnik, Maksim Stanisic, Trifko Radic, and Tomo Kovac. If you don't remember the meeting, tell us who these people are and what could they have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maksim Stanisic was president of the Executive Board of the city of Sarajevo; Trifko Radic was an MP and deputy mayor of the Serbian Sarajevo; Tomo Kovac, I'm not sure if he was the minister of MUP at the time, but he was a representative of the MUP, also from Sarajevo. I don't recall this meeting either after so many years. But the only thing this gathering could have discussed was the city of Sarajevo and the defence of the Serbian city of Sarajevo because an offensive was going on at the time and there was a great danger that the front line held by the Serb army might be broken through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we look at the entry for 18 July, that's two pages further. While we are waiting, at this meeting, was there any mention of Srebrenica and crimes in particular?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reply is the same. In my presence, there was never any talk about crimes in Srebrenica. That applies to this date and I can assert the same in relation to other dates as well, if you show them to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the 18th July now, the fourth line from the top, President Krajisnik, Tomo Kovac, Minister Ninkovic and M. Stanisic. If you can't remember the meeting, judging from the people, what could have been discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the discussion could have been identical, to do with Sarajevo issues. I was from Sarajevo, Stanisic was minister of defence, and Tomo Kovac was president of the Executive Board of the Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see the next page, please? Can you find yourself on the list?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it. I found the entry General Milosevic and President Krajisnik, 134.0 to 15.40. This seems to indicate, because General Milosevic was commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and since I was interested very much so in the defence of Sarajevo, it seems that the discussion was about the defence of Sarajevo. I don't recall the meeting, but judging from the participants, I think it could only have been about Sarajevo, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, if we could extend the session a little, I would like to try to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the last talks with Ambassador Holbrooke regarding my withdrawal from any public offices and my party positions? What was agreed and what were the time frames?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, I played the part of the main Serbian representative vis-a-vis international players, and regarding your withdrawal from the position of head of state and party positions, I spoke to Mr. Steiner and Mr. Holbrooke. And I am privy to all the details concerning that issue. But if we stop just at this meeting and the agreement with Mr. Holbrooke, this is the truth: Before Mr. Holbrooke's arrival, we had dealt with all the problems involved in the withdrawal of Mr. Karadzic with Mr. Bildt. Mr. Karadzic would hand over to Mrs. Plavsic, would not run at the next elections, and he would remain head of the party, head of the political party, because that was not a public office. That was our agreement with Mr. Bildt. Mr. Bildt then made a very unusual suggestion to me, but it was very true. He said Mr. Karadzic should go underground, he should disappear from public life. He would cease to be interesting to the international community and that would be the best indication that the implementation of the Dayton Accords is successful. Mr. Holbrooke didn't come to see us. He came to see Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Aleksa Buha and I were invited to join them in Belgrade. I don't think anyone else was invited. Mrs. Plavsic was in Pale, and Mr. Karadzic was also in Pale or somewhere else. And then, the demand came that Mr. Karadzic should also withdraw as president of his political party, to alleviate the last misgivings about the implementation of the Dayton Accords. All these talks lasted until the small hours, and what is true is that the agreement was reached at that point, Mr. Karadzic gave up on all his positions, and Mr. Holbrooke then said, As far as Mr. Karadzic is concerned, the Tribunal is --- in The Hague is history. The agreement was that the indictment would be withdrawn or it would be dealt with in some other way, and Mr. Karadzic would keep a low profile and would cease to be president of his party. And then we talked about how to make this agreement. The agreement was prepared in the sense that he was leaving all his positions and posts. But the other part was kept quiet, the part that concerned Mr. Karadzic's demands. And the reason it was kept quiet was that it was very unpopular and Mr. Holbrooke told us on the telephone that he, or the United States, should be seen as working against the Tribunal that had received international recognition. And everybody who was there can confirm what I'm saying. Why did we trust them without requiring anything on paper? First of all, we understood that secret diplomacy is one thing and public diplomacy is another thing; and the second reason is that we had great trust, great confidence, in Mr. Holbrooke. Because until that time, Mr. Holbrooke had honoured every commitment he had ever made towards us. And in his dealings with the Muslim side, he was very efficient, he settled problems very effectively, and he earned our respect. And Mr. Karadzic said, How can we not trust the man who achieved the lifting of the sanctions even before we signed anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What time frame are we talking about? When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was going on after the first post-Dayton elections, June or July 1995, after Dayton and before the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: June or July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. But I'm confusing years now. They are blending together in my mind. It was before the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much more time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems I won't be able to finish now, after all, and I will have to ask Mr. Krajisnik to come again tomorrow. But I would like to you look now at this document 1D05920. This document that deals with these meetings and then I would finish. But we can deal with this tomorrow, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although it's short, we can just identify the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will continue tomorrow morning. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
